# The formulas

<!-- Generated by electe-web/scripts/export-tools-repo.ts from electe-migration@8e52bf6 on 2026-09-29. Do not edit here: change the source and re-export. -->

One section per calculator: the formula as the page states it, the reasoning behind it, the inputs and outputs by key (the argument names `compute` takes and the keys it returns), and a worked example computed by the exported code from the example values the page shows. Percentages are returned as fractions (0.25) and shown here as percentages (25%). A division by zero or a missing input yields `null`, never `NaN` or `Infinity` — a calculator that prints "∞" has told the reader something false. The tests in `src/registry.test.ts` check each formula against a scenario with an answer somebody can verify by hand.

### ROI calculator

`roi` · Finance · [English](https://tools.electe.net/roi-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/calcolo-ritorno-investimento)

**Formula.** ROI = (amount returned − amount invested) ÷ amount invested

Enter what you put in and the total that came back — not the profit, the whole amount. The calculator subtracts one from the other itself, which is the step most ROI tools leave ambiguous: a field labelled 'profit' can mean the gain or the gross return, and the two answers differ by exactly 100 percentage points. The net gain is shown beside the percentage so you can see which number it came from.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Amount invested | `investment` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Total amount returned | `returned` | number ≥ 0 | yes |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Return on investment (headline) | `roi` | percent |
| Net gain | `netGain` | currency |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Amount invested = 10000, Total amount returned = 12500 → Return on investment = 25%, Net gain = 2500.

### NPV calculator

`npv` · Finance · [English](https://tools.electe.net/npv-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/calcolo-valore-attuale-netto)

**Formula.** NPV = Σ (cash flow ÷ (1 + rate)^year) − initial investment

Money arriving in five years is worth less than the same amount today, and the discount rate is how much less. This assumes a flat annual cash flow, which is what most small projects actually look like; a per-year grid belongs in a spreadsheet. A positive NPV means the project earns more than your discount rate demands. The payback line is undiscounted, because that is the convention — treat it as a rough second opinion, not as the answer.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial investment | `investment` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Annual cash flow | `cashflow` | number | yes |
| Years | `years` | integer ≥ 1 | yes |
| Discount rate (%) | `rate` | percent | yes |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Net present value (headline) | `npv` | currency |
| Discounted cash flows | `discounted` | currency |
| Payback (years) | `payback` | number |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Initial investment = 50000, Annual cash flow = 15000, Years = 5, Discount rate (%) = 8 → Net present value = 9890.65, Discounted cash flows = 59890.65, Payback (years) = 3.33.

### Gross margin calculator

`gross-margin` · Finance · [English](https://tools.electe.net/gross-margin-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/calcolo-margine-lordo)

**Formula.** Margin % = (revenue − COGS) ÷ revenue    ·    Markup % = (revenue − COGS) ÷ COGS

Margin is the share of the selling price you keep; markup is how much you added to the cost. On 100,000 of revenue at 60,000 of cost, the margin is 40% and the markup is 66.7% — the same trade, two numbers. Quoting one when you mean the other is the most common pricing mistake there is, so both are shown together, always.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | `revenue` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Cost of goods sold | `cogs` | number ≥ 0 | yes |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Gross margin (headline) | `marginPct` | percent |
| Gross profit | `grossProfit` | currency |
| Markup | `markupPct` | percent |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Revenue = 100000, Cost of goods sold = 62000 → Gross margin = 38%, Gross profit = 38000, Markup = 61.29%.

### Profit calculator

`profit` · Finance · [English](https://tools.electe.net/profit-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/calcolo-profitto)

**Formula.** Net profit = revenue − variable costs − fixed costs

Splitting costs into variable and fixed is what makes this more useful than subtracting one total. Variable costs move with what you sell; fixed costs are there whether you sell anything or not. The gap between revenue and variable costs is your contribution margin — the money available to cover the fixed costs, and the number that decides whether selling more actually helps.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | `revenue` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Variable costs | `variableCosts` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Fixed costs | `fixedCosts` | number ≥ 0 | yes |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Net profit (headline) | `netProfit` | currency |
| Contribution margin | `contributionMargin` | currency |
| Net margin | `netMarginPct` | percent |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Revenue = 250000, Variable costs = 120000, Fixed costs = 70000 → Net profit = 60000, Contribution margin = 130000, Net margin = 24%.

### Break-even calculator

`break-even` · Finance · [English](https://tools.electe.net/break-even-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/calcolo-punto-di-pareggio)

**Formula.** Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ (price per unit − variable cost per unit)

The denominator is your contribution per unit: what each sale leaves behind after its own costs. Divide the fixed costs by it and you get the volume at which you stop losing money. The result rounds up, because the unit that takes you from 1,142.4 to 1,143 is the one that actually crosses the line. If price is at or below variable cost the contribution is zero or negative, no volume ever breaks even, and this calculator says so instead of dividing.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total fixed costs | `fixedCosts` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Selling price per unit | `price` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Variable cost per unit | `variableCost` | number ≥ 0 | yes |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Break-even units (headline) | `breakEvenUnits` | integer |
| Break-even revenue | `breakEvenRevenue` | currency |
| Contribution per unit | `contributionPerUnit` | currency |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Total fixed costs = 40000, Selling price per unit = 90, Variable cost per unit = 55 → Break-even units = 1143, Break-even revenue = 102870, Contribution per unit = 35.

### Investment simulator

`investment-simulator` · Finance · [English](https://tools.electe.net/investment-simulator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/simulatore-investimenti)

**Formula.** Each month: value = value × (1 + monthly rate) + contribution,  monthly rate = (1 + annual return − fees)^(1/12) − 1

Contributions are added at the end of each month, which is the conservative convention and the one that matches a standing order. Fees come off the return before it compounds — a 0.5% annual fee against a 7% return means the money grows at 6.5%, every year, which over twenty years is a much larger hole than it looks. Inflation is applied to the result, not the return, so the real value line answers 'what will this buy' rather than 'what will the statement say'.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial amount | `initial` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Monthly contribution | `monthly` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Years | `years` | integer ≥ 1 | yes |
| Expected annual return (%) | `returnRate` | percent | yes |
| Average inflation (%) | `inflation` | percent | optional |
| Annual fees (%) | `fees` | percent | optional |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Final value (headline) | `finalValue` | currency |
| Value in today's money | `realValue` | currency |
| Total contributed | `contributed` | currency |
| Growth | `growth` | currency |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Initial amount = 10000, Monthly contribution = 300, Years = 15, Expected annual return (%) = 6, Average inflation (%) = 2, Annual fees (%) = 0.5 → Final value = 105009.88, Value in today's money = 78023.89, Total contributed = 64000, Growth = 41009.88.

### Net invested capital calculator

`net-invested-capital` · Finance · [English](https://tools.electe.net/net-invested-capital-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/capitale-investito-netto)

**Formula.** Net invested capital = fixed assets + (operating assets − cash − operating liabilities)

The bracket is operating working capital: what the day-to-day cycle absorbs once suppliers have financed their share. Cash is subtracted because it is not invested in operations — it is sitting there. That exclusion is the step this calculation invites people to get wrong, so cash is its own field rather than something you are expected to have already removed.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fixed assets | `fixedAssets` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Operating assets | `operatingAssets` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Operating liabilities | `operatingLiabilities` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Cash and equivalents | `cash` | number ≥ 0 | optional |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Net invested capital (headline) | `nic` | currency |
| Operating working capital | `workingCapital` | currency |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Fixed assets = 400000, Operating assets = 250000, Operating liabilities = 120000, Cash and equivalents = 60000 → Net invested capital = 470000, Operating working capital = 70000.

### Reverse factoring calculator

`reverse-factoring` · Finance · [English](https://tools.electe.net/reverse-factoring-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/reverse-factoring)

**Formula.** Discount = invoice value × rate × (days ÷ 365)

Reverse factoring lets a supplier be paid early against the buyer's credit rating rather than their own, usually at a better rate than they could get alone. The discount is priced on actual/365, the money-market convention these facilities are quoted on. The effective annual rate shows what the discount really costs the supplier once it is annualised — it is always higher than the headline rate, and that gap is the number worth checking before signing.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total invoice value | `invoiceValue` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Days paid early | `extensionDays` | integer ≥ 0 | yes |
| Discount rate (%) | `discountRate` | percent ≥ 0 | yes |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Discount cost (headline) | `financingCost` | currency |
| Net to supplier | `netToSupplier` | currency |
| Effective annual rate | `effectiveAnnualRate` | percent |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Total invoice value = 500000, Days paid early = 60, Discount rate (%) = 4.5 → Discount cost = 3698.63, Net to supplier = 496301.37, Effective annual rate = 4.53%.

### Reorder point calculator

`reorder-point` · Inventory · [English](https://tools.electe.net/reorder-point-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/punto-di-riordino)

**Formula.** Reorder point = average daily demand × lead time (days) + safety stock

The first term is how much you will sell while you wait for the delivery; the second is the cushion for when demand or the supplier misbehaves. Order when stock touches the total and, if nothing goes wrong, the delivery arrives as you reach the safety stock. Results round up: a reorder point of 337.2 means ordering at 337 leaves you short.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average daily demand | `dailyDemand` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Supplier lead time (days) | `leadTime` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Safety stock | `safetyStock` | number ≥ 0 | optional |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Reorder point (headline) | `reorderPoint` | integer |
| Demand during lead time | `leadTimeDemand` | integer |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Average daily demand = 40, Supplier lead time (days) = 7, Safety stock = 60 → Reorder point = 340, Demand during lead time = 280.

### Inventory turnover calculator

`inventory-turnover` · Inventory · [English](https://tools.electe.net/inventory-turnover-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/rotazione-scorte)

**Formula.** Turnover = COGS ÷ average inventory value    ·    Days = 365 ÷ turnover

Both figures must be at cost, not at retail — mixing a retail stock valuation with a cost of goods sold figure inflates turnover and is the most common error in this calculation. Higher turnover means less cash tied up, but pushed too far it means running out. The days figure is usually the more useful of the two because it is in units a person can picture.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cost of goods sold | `cogs` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Average inventory value | `averageInventory` | number ≥ 0 | yes |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Inventory turnover (headline) | `turnover` | number |
| Days of inventory | `daysOfInventory` | days |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Cost of goods sold = 900000, Average inventory value = 150000 → Inventory turnover = 6, Days of inventory = 60.80 days.

### Days inventory on hand

`days-inventory` · Inventory · [English](https://tools.electe.net/days-inventory-on-hand) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/giorni-di-giacenza-magazzino)

**Formula.** Days inventory = (average inventory ÷ COGS) × days in period

The same relationship as inventory turnover, expressed in days instead of turns, which is easier to act on: 'we hold sixty days of stock' says something a meeting can respond to. Set the period to match the COGS figure — 365 for a year, 90 for a quarter, 30 for a month. Using annual COGS with a 30-day period produces a number twelve times too small.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average inventory value | `averageInventory` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Cost of goods sold | `cogs` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Days in period | `periodDays` | integer ≥ 1 | yes |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Days inventory on hand (headline) | `dio` | days |
| Inventory turnover | `turnover` | number |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Average inventory value = 150000, Cost of goods sold = 900000, Days in period = 365 → Days inventory on hand = 60.80 days, Inventory turnover = 6.

### Sell-through rate calculator

`sell-through` · Inventory · [English](https://tools.electe.net/sell-through-rate-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/tasso-di-vendita-sell-through)

**Formula.** Sell-through % = units sold ÷ units received

A buying decision measure rather than an inventory one: it asks whether the quantity you committed to matched the demand that turned up. Read it against a period — 60% in four weeks and 60% in a season are different verdicts on the same buy. Results above 100% are shown rather than capped, because returns, backorders and stock transfers make them real, and a figure above 100 usually means the data needs a look rather than the buy.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Units received | `unitsReceived` | integer ≥ 0 | yes |
| Units sold | `unitsSold` | integer ≥ 0 | yes |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Sell-through rate (headline) | `sellThrough` | percent |
| Units remaining | `unitsRemaining` | integer |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Units received = 500, Units sold = 340 → Sell-through rate = 68%, Units remaining = 160.

### Average order value calculator

`aov` · Sales · [English](https://tools.electe.net/aov-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/calcolo-valore-medio-ordine)

**Formula.** Average order value = total revenue ÷ number of orders

Deceptively simple, and worth two cautions. Use net revenue after returns, or a heavy-returns category will flatter itself badly. And remember this is a mean: a handful of large orders pulls it well above what most customers actually spend, so if you are setting a free-shipping threshold from it, look at the median too.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total revenue | `revenue` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Number of orders | `orders` | integer ≥ 0 | yes |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Average order value (headline) | `aov` | currency |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Total revenue = 84000, Number of orders = 1200 → Average order value = 70.

### Sales conversion calculator

`conversion-rate` · Sales · [English](https://tools.electe.net/sales-conversion-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/calcolo-tasso-di-conversione)

**Formula.** Conversion rate = conversions ÷ total leads or visitors

The rate alone rarely changes a decision; the revenue per lead usually does, because it is what you can compare against the cost of acquiring one. If revenue per lead is above your cost per lead, spending more is arithmetic rather than a gamble. Note the rate is not rounded to whole percentages here: 3.5% and 4% differ by a seventh of your pipeline efficiency, and rounding that away has ended arguments in the wrong direction.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Conversions | `conversions` | integer ≥ 0 | yes |
| Total leads or visitors | `total` | integer ≥ 0 | yes |
| Revenue generated | `revenue` | number ≥ 0 | optional |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Conversion rate (headline) | `conversionRate` | percent |
| Revenue per lead | `revenuePerLead` | currency |
| Value per conversion | `valuePerConversion` | currency |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Conversions = 84, Total leads or visitors = 2400, Revenue generated = 42000 → Conversion rate = 3.5%, Revenue per lead = 17.50, Value per conversion = 500.

### Customer lifetime value calculator

`customer-lifetime-value` · Sales · [English](https://tools.electe.net/customer-lifetime-value-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/calcolo-valore-cliente-lifetime)

**Formula.** CLV = average order value × purchases per year × years retained

This is the revenue form, which is what the inputs describe and what most CLV tools return. It is also the optimistic one: it counts turnover, not what you keep. Enter your gross margin and the second figure shows the margin-based CLV, which is the number to compare against acquisition cost. A three-to-one ratio of margin CLV to acquisition cost is the usual rule of thumb; below one-to-one you are buying customers at a loss.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average order value | `averageOrderValue` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Purchases per year | `purchasesPerYear` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Years retained | `yearsRetained` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Gross margin (%) | `grossMargin` | percent ≥ 0 | optional |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Lifetime value (revenue) (headline) | `clv` | currency |
| Annual value | `annualValue` | currency |
| Lifetime value (margin) | `marginClv` | currency |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Average order value = 70, Purchases per year = 4, Years retained = 3, Gross margin (%) = 60 → Lifetime value (revenue) = 840, Annual value = 280, Lifetime value (margin) = 504.

### Churn rate calculator

`churn-rate` · Sales · [English](https://tools.electe.net/churn-rate-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/calcolo-tasso-di-abbandono)

**Formula.** Churn % = (customers at start + acquired − customers at end) ÷ customers at start

Losses are derived from the three counts rather than asked for directly, which matters: those numbers are usually taken from different reports, and a hand-entered churn figure that disagrees with them produces a page where the arithmetic does not hold. New customers are excluded from the denominator — churn measures whether the people you already had stayed, and folding in acquisitions lets fast growth hide a leaking bucket.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Customers at start | `customersStart` | integer ≥ 0 | yes |
| Customers at end | `customersEnd` | integer ≥ 0 | yes |
| Customers acquired | `customersAcquired` | integer ≥ 0 | optional |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Churn rate (headline) | `churnRate` | percent |
| Customers lost | `churnedCustomers` | integer |
| Retention rate | `retentionRate` | percent |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Customers at start = 1000, Customers at end = 960, Customers acquired = 120 → Churn rate = 16%, Customers lost = 160, Retention rate = 84%.

### Percentage discount calculator

`percentage-discount` · Sales · [English](https://tools.electe.net/percentage-discount-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/sconto-percentuale)

**Formula.** Saving = original price × discount %    ·    Final price = original price − saving

The simplest tool here, and the one with the most expensive mistake behind it: discounts do not stack additively. Two successive 20% reductions are not 40% off — they are 36%, because the second applies to the already-reduced price. If you are chaining promotions, run this calculator twice rather than adding the percentages.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Original price | `originalPrice` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Discount (%) | `discountPercent` | percent ≥ 0 | yes |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Final price (headline) | `finalPrice` | currency |
| You save | `saving` | currency |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Original price = 249, Discount (%) = 20 → Final price = 199.20, You save = 49.80.

### NPS calculator

`nps` · Marketing · [English](https://tools.electe.net/nps-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/net-promoter-score)

**Formula.** NPS = % promoters − % detractors    (passives count in the total, and nowhere else)

Scores of 9-10 are promoters, 7-8 passives, 0-6 detractors. Passives are the part people get wrong: they are counted in the denominator but subtracted from nothing, so a survey full of 8s produces a score near zero. That is deliberate — the metric is asking how much more advocacy than damage you have, and a satisfied-but-silent customer supplies neither. The result runs from −100 to +100 and is a count, not a percentage.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Promoters (9-10) | `promoters` | integer ≥ 0 | yes |
| Passives (7-8) | `passives` | integer ≥ 0 | yes |
| Detractors (0-6) | `detractors` | integer ≥ 0 | yes |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Net Promoter Score (headline) | `nps` | number |
| Promoters | `promoterPct` | percent |
| Detractors | `detractorPct` | percent |
| Total responses | `responses` | integer |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Promoters (9-10) = 240, Passives (7-8) = 120, Detractors (0-6) = 40 → Net Promoter Score = 50, Promoters = 60%, Detractors = 10%, Total responses = 400.

### Employee productivity calculator

`employee-productivity` · Operations · [English](https://tools.electe.net/employee-productivity-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/calcolo-produttivita-dipendente)

**Formula.** Per employee = output ÷ employees    ·    Per hour = output ÷ (employees × hours each)

Use revenue if you want a figure you can benchmark, and gross profit if you want one that means something — revenue per head flatters a business that resells at thin margins. Count full-time equivalents rather than headcount, or a team of part-timers will look twice as productive as it is. The labour ratio is output divided by the wage bill: how many units of output each unit of pay produces.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Output (revenue or gross profit) | `output` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Employees (full-time equivalent) | `employees` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Hours per employee | `hoursPerEmployee` | number ≥ 0 | optional |
| Total labour cost | `labourCost` | number ≥ 0 | optional |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Output per employee (headline) | `perEmployee` | currency |
| Output per hour | `perHour` | currency |
| Output per unit of labour cost | `labourRatio` | number |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Output (revenue or gross profit) = 800000, Employees (full-time equivalent) = 12, Hours per employee = 1600, Total labour cost = 420000 → Output per employee = 66666.67, Output per hour = 41.67, Output per unit of labour cost = 1.90.

### Renovation cost calculator

`renovation-cost` · Operations · [English](https://tools.electe.net/renovation-cost-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/costo-al-mq-ristrutturazione)

**Formula.** Total = area × rate per m² × (1 + systems %) × (1 + contingency %)

An estimate, not a quote, and the arithmetic is deliberately visible so you can argue with it. The uplifts compound rather than add: a 25% systems uplift and a 10% contingency is a 37.5% increase, not 35%. Typical Italian rates run roughly 350-600 per m² for cosmetic work, 600-1,000 for a full refurbishment, and 1,000-1,600 where layouts move and systems are replaced. Ten to fifteen per cent of contingency is normal on any building older than about forty years.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Floor area (m²) | `squareMetres` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Rate per m² | `ratePerSqm` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Systems uplift (%) | `systemsUpliftPct` | percent ≥ 0 | optional |
| Contingency (%) | `contingencyPct` | percent ≥ 0 | optional |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Estimated total (headline) | `total` | currency |
| Base cost | `baseCost` | currency |
| Effective cost per m² | `effectivePerSqm` | currency |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Floor area (m²) = 90, Rate per m² = 750, Systems uplift (%) = 25, Contingency (%) = 10 → Estimated total = 92812.50, Base cost = 67500, Effective cost per m² = 1031.25.

### Shipping cost calculator

`shipping-cost` · Operations · [English](https://tools.electe.net/shipping-cost-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/calcola-costo-spedizione)

**Formula.** Volumetric weight = (L × W × H in cm) ÷ divisor    ·    Chargeable = the greater of volumetric and actual

Carriers bill on whichever is greater: what the parcel weighs, or the space it occupies. A box of cushions weighing two kilos can be charged as nine. The divisor is the carrier's — 5000 for most European road and express services, 6000 on some air tariffs, and it is on your rate card. If your parcels are consistently charged above their weight, the cheapest saving available is a smaller box.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Length (cm) | `lengthCm` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Width (cm) | `widthCm` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Height (cm) | `heightCm` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Actual weight (kg) | `actualWeightKg` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Rate per kg | `ratePerKg` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Carrier divisor | `divisor` | integer ≥ 1 | optional |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Estimated cost (headline) | `shippingCost` | currency |
| Chargeable weight (kg) | `chargeableWeight` | number |
| Volumetric weight (kg) | `volumetricWeight` | number |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Length (cm) = 40, Width (cm) = 30, Height (cm) = 20, Actual weight (kg) = 3.5, Rate per kg = 4.2, Carrier divisor = 5000 → Estimated cost = 20.16, Chargeable weight (kg) = 4.80, Volumetric weight (kg) = 4.80.

### Cost-benefit analysis calculator

`cost-benefit` · Operations · [English](https://tools.electe.net/cost-benefit-analysis-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/analisi-costi-benefici)

**Formula.** BCR = present value of benefits ÷ present value of costs    ·    1.0 is the decision boundary

Both sides are discounted over the horizon, which is what separates this from subtracting two totals. A ratio above 1.0 means the benefits carry the costs at the rate you set; below 1.0 they do not. The ratio is more useful than the net figure when you are comparing projects of different sizes, and the net figure is more useful when you are deciding whether to do one at all — which is why both are here.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Upfront cost | `upfrontCost` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Annual running cost | `annualCost` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Annual benefit | `annualBenefit` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Years | `years` | integer ≥ 1 | yes |
| Discount rate (%) | `rate` | percent | optional |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Benefit-cost ratio (headline) | `bcr` | number |
| Net benefit | `netBenefit` | currency |
| Present value of benefits | `pvBenefits` | currency |
| Present value of costs | `pvCosts` | currency |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Upfront cost = 60000, Annual running cost = 8000, Annual benefit = 32000, Years = 5, Discount rate (%) = 6 → Benefit-cost ratio = 1.44, Net benefit = 41096.73, Present value of benefits = 134795.64, Present value of costs = 93698.91.

### Profitability calculator

`profitability` · Finance · [English](https://tools.electe.net/profitability-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/analisi-redditivita)

**Formula.** Operating profit = revenue − COGS − operating expenses    ·    ROA = operating profit ÷ total assets

Four numbers every set of accounts contains, turned into the three ratios that say whether a business is working. Gross margin is about pricing and production; net margin adds the cost of running the place; return on assets asks whether the capital sitting in the balance sheet is earning its keep. A business can have a healthy gross margin and a poor ROA, and that combination points somewhere very specific — usually at too much stock or too much unused plant.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | `revenue` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Cost of goods sold | `cogs` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Operating expenses | `operatingExpenses` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Total assets | `totalAssets` | number ≥ 0 | optional |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Net margin (headline) | `netMarginPct` | percent |
| Gross margin | `grossMarginPct` | percent |
| Operating profit | `operatingProfit` | currency |
| Return on assets | `roa` | percent |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Revenue = 1200000, Cost of goods sold = 720000, Operating expenses = 300000, Total assets = 900000 → Net margin = 15%, Gross margin = 40%, Operating profit = 180000, Return on assets = 20%.

### KPI attainment calculator

`kpi-attainment` · Operations · [English](https://tools.electe.net/kpi-attainment-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/gestione-kpi)

**Formula.** Attainment = actual ÷ target    ·    Progress from baseline = (actual − baseline) ÷ (target − baseline)

Attainment against a target is the headline, but it is often misleading on its own: if you started the quarter at 60 and the target is 100, being at 84 is 84% attainment and 60% of the distance you actually had to travel. The baseline field is what separates those two readings. It works for lower-is-better targets too — set the baseline above the target and the progress figure still reads correctly.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Current value | `actual` | number | yes |
| Target | `target` | number | yes |
| Starting baseline | `baseline` | number | optional |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Attainment (headline) | `attainment` | percent |
| Remaining gap | `gap` | number |
| Progress from baseline | `progressFromBaseline` | percent |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Current value = 84, Target = 100, Starting baseline = 60 → Attainment = 84%, Remaining gap = 16, Progress from baseline = 60%.

### Domestic worker holiday calculator

`domestic-worker-holiday` · Operations · [English](https://tools.electe.net/domestic-worker-holiday-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/ferie-per-colf-a-ore)

**Formula.** Days = 26 × (months worked ÷ 12) × (weekly hours ÷ full-time hours)

The Italian collective agreement for domestic work gives 26 working days of paid holiday a year, accrued monthly and pro-rated by hours for part-time staff. A month worked for fifteen days or more counts as a whole month. Full-time here means 40 hours a week for live-out staff and 54 for live-in, so set that field to match the contract — using 40 for a live-in worker overstates the entitlement by a third.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hours worked per week | `hoursPerWeek` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Months worked this year | `monthsWorked` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Full-time hours per week | `fullTimeHours` | number ≥ 1 | optional |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Holiday days accrued (headline) | `holidayDays` | number |
| Approximate hours | `holidayHours` | number |
| Accrual per month | `accrualPerMonth` | number |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Hours worked per week = 20, Months worked this year = 12, Full-time hours per week = 40 → Holiday days accrued = 13, Approximate hours = 43.30, Accrual per month = 1.08.

### Variance calculator

`variance` · Data · [English](https://tools.electe.net/variance-calculator-online) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/calcolo-varianza)

**Formula.** Population variance = Σ(x − mean)² ÷ n    ·    Sample variance = Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1)

Both conventions are always shown, because picking one blind is the mistake this calculator exists to prevent. Divide by n when your list is the entire population you care about; divide by n−1 when it is a sample and you are estimating a wider population's variance. The n−1 version is always slightly larger, and with small lists the gap is substantial — on eight values it is about 14%.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Sample variance (headline) | `sampleVariance` | number |
| Population variance | `populationVariance` | number |
| Mean | `mean` | number |
| Sample standard deviation | `sampleStdDev` | number |
| Values | `count` | integer |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows):  → Sample variance = —, Population variance = —, Mean = —, Sample standard deviation = —, Values = 0.

### Reclassified balance sheet

`balance-sheet-reclassification` · Finance · [English](https://tools.electe.net/reclassified-balance-sheet) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/stato-patrimoniale-riclassificato-schema)

**Formula.** Working capital = current assets − short-term debt    ·    Treasury margin = (receivables + cash) − short-term debt    ·    Structural margin = equity − fixed assets

The statutory layout is built for filing, not for reading. Reclassifying it by liquidity produces three margins that answer three different questions. Working capital asks whether short-term assets cover short-term debt. Treasury margin asks the same thing without counting stock — the harder question, and the one working capital quietly answers 'yes' to. Structural margin asks whether your own money covers your long-term investment, or whether the bank is funding the building.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fixed assets | `fixedAssets` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Inventory | `inventory` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Receivables | `receivables` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Cash and equivalents | `cash` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Equity | `equity` | number | yes |
| Short-term liabilities | `shortTermDebt` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Long-term liabilities | `longTermDebt` | number ≥ 0 | yes |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Working capital (headline) | `workingCapital` | currency |
| Treasury margin | `treasuryMargin` | currency |
| Structural margin | `structuralMargin` | currency |
| Current ratio | `currentRatio` | number |
| Current assets | `currentAssets` | currency |
| Debt to equity | `debtToEquity` | number |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Fixed assets = 380000, Inventory = 90000, Receivables = 140000, Cash and equivalents = 45000, Equity = 300000, Short-term liabilities = 210000, Long-term liabilities = 145000 → Working capital = 65000, Treasury margin = -25000, Structural margin = -80000, Current ratio = 1.31, Current assets = 275000, Debt to equity = 1.18.

### Business lease calculator

`business-lease` · Finance · [English](https://tools.electe.net/business-lease-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/affitto-di-azienda)

**Formula.** Annual rent = value of assets leased × expected yield    ·    Sanity check = rent ÷ EBITDA

Two anchors, because either alone misleads. The yield anchor prices the rent as a return on the capital handed over — plant, fittings, stock, goodwill. The EBITDA check asks what share of the earnings that rent consumes. A rent that looks fair as a yield and takes 80% of EBITDA is a business the tenant cannot run, and it is the number a first-time lessee never works out. This is an indication for a negotiation, not a valuation: an actual affitto d'azienda is a notarised contract and the figure belongs to a professional.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Value of assets leased | `assetValue` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Annual revenue | `revenue` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Annual operating costs | `operatingCosts` | number ≥ 0 | yes |
| Expected yield (%) | `yieldPct` | percent ≥ 0 | yes |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Indicative annual rent (headline) | `annualRent` | currency |
| Monthly rent | `monthlyRent` | currency |
| EBITDA | `ebitda` | currency |
| Rent as share of EBITDA | `rentToEbitda` | percent |
| Left to the tenant | `residualToTenant` | currency |

**Worked example** (the example values the page shows): Value of assets leased = 450000, Annual revenue = 620000, Annual operating costs = 540000, Expected yield (%) = 7 → Indicative annual rent = 31500, Monthly rent = 2625, EBITDA = 80000, Rent as share of EBITDA = 39.38%, Left to the tenant = 48500.

### Sales forecast calculator

`sales-forecast` · Sales · [English](https://tools.electe.net/sales-forecast-calculator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/previsione-vendite)

**Formula.** level = α·actual + (1−α)·(level + trend)    ·    trend = β·(level change) + (1−β)·trend    ·    forecast(h) = level + h·trend

This is Holt's linear trend — double exponential smoothing — which is what most 'AI sales forecasting' turns out to be once you open it. Alpha decides how much the newest figure moves the level; beta how much it moves the trend. Higher values react faster and are noisier. It deliberately does NOT fit seasonality: that needs at least two full cycles of history, and a tool that silently fits a season to eight months of data produces confident nonsense. If your business is seasonal, forecast against the same period last year rather than the month just gone.

| input | key | kind | required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Periods to forecast | `periodsAhead` | integer ≥ 1 | yes |
| Level smoothing (α, 0-1) | `alpha` | number ≥ 0 | optional |
| Trend smoothing (β, 0-1) | `beta` | number ≥ 0 | optional |
| the pasted series | `series` | numbers | yes |

| output | key | format |
|---|---|---|
| Next period (headline) | `next` | number |
| Total over the horizon | `total` | number |
| Trend per period | `trend` | number |
| Current level | `level` | number |
| History points | `periods` | integer |

**Worked examples** for series tools are in `src/registry.test.ts`.
